This is not necessarily true. Likewise sex and gender are not synonymous in all cases. Genotypic sex, phenotypic sex, and brain sex can vary independently. I suppose how "gender" is defined would matter, but I usually use it to describe brain sex.

Different part of the body can exhibit different abnormalities during development.

Take for instance the case of individuals with androgen insensitivity syndrome. The have a male genotype (XY), an extremely female phenotype, and their brain sex/gender/whatever can vary though is usually female.

It is also possible for a person to have the male genotype, exhibit a masculine phenotype (looks like a male/have a penis), but due to altered prenatal exposure to hormones have a "female" brain. A brain that in every distinguishable sense is female.

It is thought that a less extreme form of this process is what results in homosexual individuals, where only portions of brain development are subjected to altered hormone concentrations.

You can actually replicate this process intentionally with lab animals. Creating mice of one genotypic sex, who express the concurrent phenotypic sex but behave as the other sex and whose brain structure is that of the other sex as well.

Remember, all humans start female, hormonal expression is what turns some into males, this process doesn't always work "as planned."

Whether all humans who identify as transgender share this state is unknown.

Now, whether it is realistic for transgender individuals of any sort to believe they can change their phenotypic sex is I suppose a matter of personal aesthetic, societal interpretation, and the current state of technology.
